policy_title: Initial Preventive Physical Examination and Annual Wellness Visit

extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, an initial preventive physical examination (IPPE), also known as the "Welcome to Medicare" preventive visit, is a one-time introductory visit provided during the first 12 months a Medicare beneficiary has Part B benefits. The visit may include, but is not limited to, the following: • A review of a beneficiary's medical and health-related social history. • Education and counseling about preventive services, including certain screenings, shots and referrals for other care, if needed. • Other services, such as a written plan letting the beneficiary know what preventive services the beneficiary needs. If a beneficiary has had Part B benefits for longer than 12 months, the beneficiary can receive an annual wellness visit (AWV) to develop or update a personalized prevention plan to prevent disease and disability based on the beneficiary’s current health and risk factors. The following policy outlines Humana’s reimbursement for claims for an IPPE and AWV.

extracted_content.title: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy
extracted_content.content: In addition to the policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements. Humana Medicare Advantage plans reimburse a charge for: • An IPPE service, HCPCS code G0402 , once per lifetime and only if provided within the first 12 months after the effective date of the member’s first Medicare Part B coverage period. • An initial AWV service, HCPCS code G0438 , once per lifetime beginning in the calendar year following the IPPE. However, the initial AWV is not dependent on reimbursement of an earlier IPPE. • A subsequent AWV service, HCPCS code G0439 , once per calendar year beginning in the calendar year following an allowed charge for HCPCS code G0438 . However, a subsequent AWV is not dependent on reimbursement of an earlier AWV or IPPE. Humana limits reimbursement of HCPCS codes G0402, G0438 and G0439 to only one of these services per calendar year.

extracted_content.content: Bilateral procedures are procedures that are performed on similar sites on opposite sides of the body, during the same session, by the same qualified health care practitioner. When a procedure reported using a service code with a Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS) Relative Value File (RVF) bilateral indicator 1 is performed bilaterally, providers must report the code with either modifier 50 or with anatomical modifiers such as modifiers LT and RT . Humana strongly encourages providers to report a bilateral procedure using modifier 50 rather than modifiers LT and RT , but accepts both methods. When using modifier 50 to report a bilateral procedure, report a single claim line with a unit of 1. When using modifiers LT and RT to report a bilateral procedure, report two claim lines, each with a unit of 1. Only report modifier 50 when the procedure is performed on similar but opposite sites. For example, report modifier 50 for the same service code for a procedure performed on the right and left knee. However, do not report modifier 50 for the same service code for a procedure performed on the right knee and left shoulder. When reporting two or more bilateral procedures using the same code, report the first bilateral procedure on a single claim line with a unit of 1 using modifier 50 and report a single claim line with a unit of 1 for all subsequent bilateral procedures using modifier 50 and modifier 59. It is not necessary to report modifier 50 with a service code with an MPFS RVF bilateral indicator other than 1.

extracted_content.content: In some situations, it is necessary for two surgeons to work together, each as a primary surgeon, on the same patient during the same operative session due to factors such as the complexity of the procedure or the condition of the patient. This can include surgeries when two surgeons of different specialties are required for a specific procedure. This can also include surgeries in which two surgeons perform elements of the procedure simultaneously such as during bilateral knee replacement or a heart transplant. In such circumstances, the physicians are considered co-surgeons, not assistant surgeons. Note: Surgeons of different specialties performing distinct procedures, even if the procedures use the same incision site, are not considered co-surgeons.

extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has directed providers to use modifier CT to report computed tomography (CT) services furnished on equipment that is not consistent with dose optimization standards established by the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA). Enforcement of NEMA Standard XR 29-2013, also known as the MITA Smart Dose standard, for the Medicare Program is required by the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014. The criteria of NEMA Standard XR 29-2013 ensure use of the lowest radiation dose necessary to get the image quality needed by providers to make a proper diagnosis. The standard outlines four attributes CT equipment should meet to ensure that a patient receives the highest standard of care as established by professional societies and regulatory agencies. Performing CT services on equipment that meets all elements of the standard helps reduce a patient’s lifetime exposure to potentially cancer-causing medical radiation. Humana works to reduce our members’ exposure to medical radiation. Directly and through vendor partnerships, we educate our members on the risks of medical radiation exposure and encourage our in-network providers to provide high quality advanced diagnostic services that meet a broad set of industry standards, including NEMA Standard XR 29-2013. This policy outlines Humana’s billing requirements and reimbursement for services reported with modifier CT .

In situations in which, for a global surgical package that may be split, there is an agreed transfer of care, it is appropriate to reimburse the various practitioners for portions of the global surgical package . Humana allows a charge for preoperative management only, indicated by modifier 56 , at the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan for the service multiplied by that service’s MPFS preoperative percentage. Humana allows a charge for intraoperative care only, indicated by modifier 54 , at the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan for the service multiplied by that service’s MPFS intraoperative percentage. Humana allows a charge for postoperative management only, as indicated by modifier 55 , at the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan for the service, multiplied by that service’s MPFS postoperative percentage, and multiplied by the percentage of the global surgery period for which the billing practitioner provided care. Effectively, the total of all percentages of a global surgery period for which practitioners were responsible for postoperative management is 100%. Therefore, the plan does not allow more than 100% of the postoperative management for that service. Humana expects a practitioner to report, in the units field on the claim form, the number of days of service that the practitioner provided, consistent with the transfer of postoperative management to which the practitioners agreed. However, if a Medicare A/B MAC directs providers to report the number of days differently, Humana MA plans permit out-of-network providers in the jurisdiction to report days consistent with the MAC 's guidance. Humana considers a charge submitted with modifier 54 as a charge for both preoperative management and intraoperative care , unless there is a coverable charge for the same procedure code for preoperative management only, as indicated by modifier 56 . If there is a coverable charge submitted with modifier 56 for the same service, the plan considers a charge submitted with modifier 54 as a charge for intraoperative care only.

extracted_content.content: In addition to the policy, claims payments are subject to other plan requirements for the processing and payment of claims, including, but not limited to, requirements of medical necessity and reasonableness and applicable referral or authorization requirements. Humana expects each healthcare provider to administer drugs and biologicals, collectively referred to as drugs, efficiently and in a clinically appropriate manner. This includes using multi-dose vials or packages when available and clinically appropriate. Humana also expects providers to use the combination of available single-dose vials or packages that results in the least amount of discarded drug. For example, if: • A drug is only available in single-dose 500 milligram and 120 milligram vials, • 540 milligrams are administered, and • The Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) code defines one base unit of the code as 10 milligrams, Then five of the 120 milligram vials should be used, resulting in a discarded amount of 60 milligrams (6 units). It is not appropriate to use a combination of one 500 milligram vial and one 120 milligram vial, resulting in a discarded amount of 80 milligrams (8 units). Humana reimburses for the discarded amount of a drug when all of the following criteria are satisfied: • The drug is a covered expense, • The discarded amount is the remainder of a single-dose vial or package used to treat the patient, and • The drug is billed as described below. When those criteria are satisfied, Humana reimburses no more, for the total administered and total discarded, for a drug than the amount appropriate, in dollars, for the efficient administration amount of the drug.

extracted_content.title: Billing For a Discarded Amount
extracted_content.section: Medicare Advantage and Commercial Payment Policy
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage and Commercial Payment Policy > Billing For a Discarded Amount
extracted_content.content: When there is a discarded amount of drug from a single-dose vial or package, Humana expects providers to report modifier JW according to applicable Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) guidance. When, as discussed above, a discarded amount is reimbursable for a date of service, the billing provider must submit two lines, as described below, using the HCPCS code appropriate for that drug for that date of service: The number of base units submitted for each of the two lines must be calculated using the appropriate unit size indicated by the HCPCS code description. The first of the two lines must indicate the number of base units appropriate for the amount administered to the patient, with fractions rounded up to the next highest whole number of base units . For example, if: • 14 milligrams are administered and • The HCPCS code defines one base unit of the code as 10 milligrams, Then the first of the two lines must indicate 2 units of the HCPCS code because the 14 milligrams administered are one base unit of the HCPCS code and a fraction of a second base unit of the HCPCS code. The second of the two lines, with modifier JW appended, must indicate the number of base units that is the difference between the efficient administration amount and the number of base units indicated on the first of the two lines. Continuing the example above, if: • 14 milligrams are administered, • The HCPCS code defines one base unit of the code as 10 milligrams, and • Of the vials available for provider purchase, the amount that results in the least amount of discarded drug is one 30 milligram vial Then the second of the two lines must indicate 1 unit of the HCPCS code because • The efficient administration amount is 30 milligrams, • The number of base units for the efficient administration amount is 3, and • The difference between the number of base units for the efficient administration amount (3) and the number of base units indicated on the first of the two lines (2) is 1. For each of those two lines, the provider must submit a charge amount that is the charge amount applicable per base unit multiplied by the number of base units indicated for that line. Continuing the example above: For each drug with a reimbursable discarded amount for a date of service, the combined amount charged for both lines must not exceed the total charge that would be appropriate if, for the efficient administration amount , the provider had administered all of each vial or package used. If the number of base units that would be appropriate for the billing of the first of two lines equals the number of base units for the efficient administration amount , then, instead of submitting two lines, the provider submits only one line with modifier JZ . For example, if: • 40 milligrams are administered, • The HCPCS code defines one base unit of the code as 25 milligrams, and • Of the vials available for provider purchase, the amount that results in the least amount of discarded drug is two 25 milligram vials, Then only one line is submitted and must indicate 2 units of the HCPCS code because the 40 milligrams administered are one base unit of the HCPCS code and a fraction of a second base unit of the HCPCS code. Suppliers who dispense but do not administer drugs from single-dose vials and packages should report modifier JW when there was a discarded amount of drug during the preparation process before supplying the drug. In addition to the limitations described above, Humana will deny a line reported with modifier JW when: • The billing provider submitted the line with a procedure code that is not a drug code, • The billing provider submitted that line to report a multi-dose vial or package, • The billing provider did not also submit a line for the administered amount, without modifier JW , for the same drug code and date of service, or • The combined number of units submitted for both lines exceeds the total base units for the efficient administration amount .

extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: This policy outlines various multiple procedure payment reductions (MPPR). Practitioner reimbursement for a procedure code generally includes reimbursement for the individual costs, also known as inputs, typically associated with that service. For example, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) uses a formula that accounts for the inputs associated with a procedure code to determine Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS) reimbursement rates for that code. When the same provider renders multiple services, or multiple units of the same service, to the same patient on the same day, the total calculation for the procedure code(s) could account more than once for an input that was only rendered once. Examples of inputs that might be contemplated in reimbursement for certain procedure codes, that would not typically be duplicated in the same encounter include: greeting and gowning the patient; preparing the room, equipment and supplies; providing education and obtaining consent. An MPPR adjusts reimbursement to offset duplication of reimbursement for inputs that were only rendered once.

extracted_content.content: Diagnostic Imaging Services Technical Component For diagnostic imaging services, the portion of an in-network practitioner’s contracted rate that is attributable to the TC may be subject to MPPR. For diagnostic imaging services rendered by an out-of-network practitioner, the portion of the base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to the TC may be subject to MPPR. For reimbursement of only a TC , all of the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan is attributable to the TC . For reimbursement of both a TC and a PC , the portion of the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to the TC is that rate or amount multiplied by the ratio of the code’s MPFS local TC amount to the code’s MPFS local global amount. Humana applies an MPPR to same-day diagnostic imaging TC services rendered by the same provider . To determine whether the MPPR applies to a specific allowed charge or to one or more units of a charge with multiple allowed units: First, of the services for which Humana is reimbursing for a TC , Humana identifies the same-day services with a MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 4. Second, Humana ranks all identified services from highest dollar amount to lowest dollar amount. We rank by the portion of the charge’s per-unit practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to TC , as described above. Finally, Humana eliminates from review the unit of service that is ranked highest; or, if multiple units of service are ranked highest, Humana eliminates one of those units. Humana applies MPPR to all other allowed units of service. When Humana determines to apply diagnostic imaging services TC MPPR to a unit, a 50 percent reduction is applied to the reimbursement for the portion of the unit’s practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to TC . Note: In certain circumstances, additional payment rules may apply. Diagnostic Imaging Professional Component For diagnostic imaging services, the portion of an in-network practitioner’s contracted rate that is attributable to the PC may be subject to MPPR. For diagnostic imaging services rendered by an out-of-network practitioner, the portion of the base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to the PC may be subject to MPPR. For reimbursement of only a PC , all of the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan is attributable to the PC . For reimbursement of both a PC and a TC , the portion of the contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to the PC is that rate or amount multiplied by the ratio of the code’s MPFS local PC amount to the code’s MPFS local global amount. Humana applies an MPPR to same-day diagnostic imaging PC services rendered by the same provider . To determine whether the MPPR applies to a specific allowed charge or to one or more units of a charge with multiple allowed units: First, of the services for which Humana is reimbursing for a PC , Humana identifies the same-day services with a MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 4. Second, Humana ranks all identified services from highest dollar amount to lowest dollar amount. We rank by the portion of the charge’s per-unit practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to PC , as described above. Finally, Humana eliminates from review the unit of service that is ranked highest; or, if multiple units of service are ranked highest, Humana eliminates one of those units. Humana applies MPPR to all other allowed units of service. When Humana determines to apply diagnostic imaging services PC MPPR to a unit: • For dates of service on or after January 1, 2017, a 5 percent reduction is applied to the reimbursement for the portion of the unit’s practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to PC . • For dates of service before January 1, 2017, a 25 percent reduction is applied to the reimbursement for the portion of the unit’s practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to PC . Note: In certain circumstances, additional payment rules may apply. Diagnostic Imaging Technical and Professional Component Any charge could be subject to a TC MPPR, PC MPPR or both. When both TC MPPR and PC MPPR are applied, calculation of the TC MPPR is separate from calculation of the PC MPPR. The rankings of TC and PC are independent of each other. For example: First, of the services for which Humana is reimbursing for a TC and PC , Humana identifies the same-day services with a MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 4. Second, Humana ranks all identified services from highest dollar amount to lowest dollar amount. We rank by the portion of the charge’s per-unit practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to TC and PC separately, as described above. Finally, Humana eliminates from review the unit of service that is ranked highest for TC and PC separately. Humana applies TC MPPR and PC MPPR separately to all other allowed units of service. When Humana determines to apply diagnostic imaging services TC MPPR to a unit, a 50 percent reduction is applied to the reimbursement for the portion of the unit’s practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to TC . When Humana determines to apply diagnostic imaging services PC MPPR to a unit, for dates of service on or after January 1, 2017, a 5 percent reduction is applied to the reimbursement for the portion of the unit’s practitioner’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan that is attributable to PC .

extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy > Multiple Endoscopic Procedures
extracted_content.content: For endoscopic services rendered by an in-network practitioner, the contracted rate may be subject to MPPR. For endoscopic services rendered by an out-of-network practitioner, the base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan may be subject to MPPR. Humana applies an MPPR to same-family endoscopic procedures, including multiple units of the same procedure code, rendered by the same provider on the same day. To determine whether the MPPR applies to a specific allowed charge: First, of the services for which Humana is reimbursing, Humana identifies, for a date of service, all MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 3 endoscopy codes and identifies each service’s base endoscopy code. Second, Humana groups all services with the same endoscopy base code. Each group of services with the same base code is one endoscopic family. Third, when there are multiple procedure codes for an endoscopic family and one of those is the family’s base code, Humana denies separate reimbursement for that base code charge. Reimbursement for the base code is included in reimbursement for the highest ranked procedure code in that endoscopic family. Humana ranks all reimbursable services within each endoscopic family by the procedure’s contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan . Finally, within each endoscopic family, Humana reduces reimbursement for each procedure code, except that family’s highest ranked procedure. The amount Humana uses to reduce reimbursement for a procedure code is the amount allowed for the procedure’s base code. When a contracted rate does not include an amount allowed for a base code, Humana will apply the following formula based on amounts provided by CMS. These amounts are used to create a reduction amount. The reduction amount is then applied to the contracted rate. Endoscopic procedures are also subject to multiple surgery reduction. As discussed in the Multiple Surgery section below, each endoscopic family is treated as a single surgery for determination of a multiple surgery reduction. information.

extracted_content.title: Multiple Surgery
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage Payment Policy > Multiple Surgery
extracted_content.content: Humana applies a multiple surgery reduction when: • The same provider performs more than one same-day MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 2 service; or • The same provider performs endoscopic procedures in more than one endoscopic family on the same day (see Multiple Endoscopic Procedures section above); or • The same provider performs at least one MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 2 service and at least one endoscopic procedure on the same day. In unique circumstances, for the purposes of applying a multiple surgery reduction: • Humana may not consider an MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator 2 service as a surgery. • Humana may consider a service that does not have an MPFS Relative Value File multiple procedure indicator of 2 as a surgery. Multiple surgery reduction applies to same-day services whether or not those services were submitted with modifier 51 , modifier 59 or modifiers X{EPSU}. Humana plans apply a multiple surgery reduction as follows: • The procedure with the highest contracted rate or base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan is not reduced; and • All other procedures are reduced by 50 percent. Special Rules for Endoscopic Services For an endoscopic service, multiple endoscopy reduction and multiple surgery reduction are determined separately. This will result in one of the following scenarios, depending on the number of services billed and the individual multiple procedure indicator code of each service : • Multiple endoscopy reduction alone could apply to the service. • Multiple surgery reduction alone could apply to the service. • Both multiple endoscopy reduction and multiple surgery reduction could apply to the service. • Neither multiple endoscopy reduction nor multiple surgery reduction could apply to the service. If multiple endoscopy reduction applies, it is always determined before multiple surgery reduction. After determining any multiple endoscopy reductions, all endoscopic services in the same endoscopic family are treated as a single service for the purpose of determining multiple surgery reduction, as follows: • For multiple surgery reduction ranking purposes, endoscopic procedures in the same endoscopic family are treated as one service. • An endoscopic family’s multiple surgery reduction ranking establishes the multiple surgery reduction percentage, if any, for all services in that endoscopic family. Note : Additional payment rules may apply in certain circumstances. For example, when a bilateral adjustment is applicable, it will be applied before a multiple surgery reduction.

extracted_content.title: Definitions of Italicized Terms
extracted_content.content: • Always Therapy: A service that is always considered a therapy, as noted in the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS) Relative Value File by a multiple procedure indicator 5. • Base maximum amount payable under the member’s plan: The maximum amount of reimbursement for a unit of a covered expense, determined by the member’s plan. Depending on the plan, this may be the maximum allowable fee, the appropriate Medicare fee schedule rate or an amount derived from another payment model. Actual plan reimbursement may be less than this base maximum amount, because of applicable adjustments. • Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS) Relative Value File: A file published by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services that includes, among other information, multiple procedure indicator, relative value units and conversion factors for practitioner services. This file is commonly referred to as the relative value unit (RVU) table. Elements of the file that are referenced in this policy include the following: – CF: The conversion factor is the amount shown in the MPFS Relative Value File for the appropriate year. – PE GPCI: The practice expense geographic price index for the area where the service was rendered, shown in the MPFS Relative Value File for the appropriate year. – PE RVU: The practice expense relative value unit is the amount shown in the MPFS Relative Value File for the appropriate year. • Modifier 26: Professional component. • Modifier 51: Multiple procedures. • Modifier 59: Distinct procedural service. • Modifier TC: Technical component. • Modifiers X{EPSU}: Modifiers XE, XP, XS and XU, collectively. – Modifier XE : Separate encounter. – Modifier XP : Separate practitioner. – Modifier XS : Separate structure. – Modifier XU : Unusual non-overlapping service. • Practice Expense (PE): One of three groups of inputs used to determine pricing of services covered under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS); PE accounts for costs of running a practice (other than expenses associated with professional liability and the practitioner’s actual work), including rent, equipment, supplies and staff costs other than the work performed by the practitioner personally. • Professional Component (PC): The professional component of a service is for practitioner work interpreting a diagnostic test or performing a procedure and includes indirect practice and malpractice expenses related to that work. • Same Provider: A single qualified practitioner or multiple practitioners within the same group practice. • Technical Component (TC): The technical component of a service is for all non-practitioner work and includes administrative, personnel and capital (equipment and facility) costs and related malpractice expenses.

extracted_content.title: Overview
extracted_content.content: The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) provides continuous care to a critically ill neonate and involves many advanced technologies and interventions that are unique to the specialty area. These critically ill neonates can suffer from various medical conditions including congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, prematurity, respiratory distress, metabolic disorders and difficulties with feeding and growth. Diagnosis related groups (DRGs), including Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Groups (MS-DRGs) and All Patient Refined Diagnosis Related Groups (APR-DRGs), are assigned to newborns based on factors including, but not limited to, birth weight, extent of prematurity, diagnoses, severity of illness, and associated significant problems. NICU is comprised of four levels of care: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 and Level 4. Each of the four levels of care has a corresponding revenue code: 0171, 0172, 0173 and 0174, respectively. This policy outlines Humana’s billing requirements and reimbursement for NICU claims. Please note the definitions and background information for the following terms that are relevant for this policy: • Neonate: An infant who is less than four weeks old. • Prematurity: The condition when a neonate is born before a gestational age of 37 weeks and zero days. • Extreme prematurity: The condition when a neonate is born before a gestational age of 28 weeks and zero days. • Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) (ICD-10-CM diagnosis code P22.0): Occurs when there is a deficiency of

Prematurity is the primary cause as surfactant production by the lungs does not occur until around a gestational age of 26 weeks, so the majority of cases are seen in the extreme premature

extracted_content.content: population. In total, all case-types of newborn respiratory distress occurs in approximately 7 percent of deliveries with only about 1 percent resulting in RDS. Prematurity and low birth weight are the most important risk factors in the development of RDS and usually occurs before a gestational age of 28 weeks. Chest X-ray findings for RDS are classic. The findings include diffuse atelectasis, with a ground-glass appearance, air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Treatment includes surfactant therapy; assisted ventilation with a ventilator, continuous positive airway pressure (regular or nasal), or other assisted ventilation such as high flow oxygen; monitoring of oxygenation; and supportive care (thermoregulation, nutritional support, fluid and electrolyte management, etc.) • Transient tachypnea of the newborn (ICD-10-CM diagnosis code P22.1): A transient respiratory distress caused when fetal lung fluid that is not readily absorbed from the lungs during the delivery process. Chest X-ray findings show lungs that are normal or hyperinflated. There is noted perihilar streaking, and the lung fissures can demonstrate fluid in them. Treatment is oxygen and supportive care. This typically resolves within a few days. • Other respiratory distress of newborn (ICD-10-CM diagnosis code P22.8): Respiratory distress that occurs in the neonatal period that is related to a specific disease process. Examples include respiratory distress secondary to pneumonia, sepsis, meconium aspiration, congenital heart defect, etc. • Respiratory distress of newborn, unspecified (ICD-10-CM diagnosis code P22.9): Respiratory distress that occurs in the neonatal period that is not related to a specific identified disease process or does not meet the definition of transient tachypnea of the newborn or RDS. extracted_content.title: Billing of Observation Services
extracted_content.section: Medicare Advantage and Medicaid Payment Policy
extracted_content.hierarchy_path: Medicare Advantage and Medicaid Payment Policy > Billing of Observation Services
extracted_content.content: The billing of facility observation services is appropriate only when the observation services were medically necessary, the observation services were ordered by a qualified healthcare professional , the patient was under the care of a physician or qualified nonphysician practitioner during observation services, and one or more of the following is true of the encounter: • Treatment and monitoring were provided to determine if inpatient admission was needed • The observation services were provided for patient monitoring, after outpatient surgery or diagnostic testing, that was beyond the standard recovery period for the service • A qualified healthcare professional directly referred the patient to the facility for observation services • The patient was a child who was observed because of an uncertain clinical response to outpatient therapy • The patient was a child whose parent or caregiver was unavailable or unknown If none of those events occurred, a Humana plan does not reimburse for a facility observation charge. The billing of and reimbursement for observation services are limited to rendered observation services that were specifically medically necessary and typically do not exceed 48 hours. Any time for any of the following scenarios is excluded from the calculation of billable observation hours: • Patient monitoring during diagnostic or therapeutic services, including observation care interrupted by such services • Routine preparation for outpatient surgery and diagnostic testing • Services provided during the standard recovery period after outpatient surgery, which is four to six hours, or after diagnostic testing • Services provided for the convenience of the patient, physician or qualified nonphysician practitioner • Observation services provided according to a standing order • The time period between the order for observation services and when observation services began • The time period between observation services ending and the patient’s discharge • The time period between observation services ending and the arrival of the patient’s transportation

It is most often used as a screening procedure to look for early signs of cancer in the colon or rectum. However, the test may reveal inflamed tissue, abnormal growths and ulcers. This policy describes Humana's billing expectation for distinguishing between a screening colonoscopy and a screening colonoscopy that results in a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure.

extracted_content.content: For dates of service beginning January 1, 2020, Humana MA plans also allow certain additional telehealth services that are not Original Medicare telehealth services . Additional telehealth services must meet the following criteria: • The service must be one of those covered under the additional telehealth service benefit in the member’s applicable Evidence of Coverage. • The service must be provided by a physician or other qualified healthcare practitioner that has satisfied Humana’s telehealth credentialing and recredentialing standards and has a valid and effective contract with Humana. • The service must be provided by a physician or other qualified healthcare practitioner that satisfies the following requirements: – Meets all applicable licensure, certification and registration requirements, including Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) registration, if applicable, in the state(s) in which they practice and the state in which the patient is located at the time of the encounter; – Is operating within the scope of their license; and – Meets professional practice standards in the state(s) in which they practice and the state in which the patient is located at the time of the encounter. • The service must be provided using real-time interactive audio technology, and Humana encourages providers to simultaneously use real-time interactive video technology, when appropriate. For a charge for a particular service to be reimbursed, it must be possible to provide all the necessary components of the code with the real-time interactive technology used. • The physician or other qualified healthcare practitioner must verify the member’s identity before providing the service. • The Humana member must provide verbal or written consent to receive the service, in accordance with state law. • The Humana member must be present for the full duration of the service. Services not meeting the criteria outlined above will not be allowed by Humana as additional telehealth services . Unless prohibited by applicable federal statute or regulation, Humana plans allow additional telehealth services if it is medically appropriate to furnish the service via telecommunications-based technology, the service is coverable by the plan, and all applicable coding requirements are satisfied. For further information on the service codes that may be reported as additional telehealth services , see the Medicare Advantage Additional Telehealth Services Benefit Code List section of the policy.
